Distribution functions for meta-d' SDT

Source: R/distributions.R
sdt_metad_dist.Rd

Density and random generation for the meta-d' model (Maniscalco & Lau, 2012). Confidence thresholds are placed using the metacognitive sensitivity metad, then rescaled so the total "old"/"new" response rates match what type-1 d predicts. These are the simulation counterparts of the metad version of sdt_rating(). The old/new boundary is the middle threshold, so the number of rating categories must be even (an odd number of thresholds).

Usage

dsdt_metad(
  counts,
  stimulus,
  d,
  thresholds,
  metad,
  sdratio = 1,
  dist = c("normal", "gumbel_min", "gumbel_max", "logistic"),
  log = FALSE
)

rsdt_metad(
  n,
  n_trials,
  stimulus,
  d,
  thresholds,
  metad,
  sdratio = 1,
  dist = c("normal", "gumbel_min", "gumbel_max", "logistic")
)

Arguments

counts

Integer matrix with one row per observation and one column per rating category, ordered from "definitely noise" (1) to "definitely signal" (K), or a vector for a single observation. A data frame is read as the matrix of its rows.

stimulus

Integer vector (0/1). Stimulus type: 0 = noise, 1 = signal.

d

Numeric vector. Sensitivity: \(d'\) when sdratio is 1, and otherwise the balanced index \(d_a\) (see sdt_yn()). The separation between the distributions in noise units is d * sqrt((1 + sdratio^2) / 2).

thresholds

Numeric vector of length K-1 with the ordered decision thresholds, or an n-by-(K-1) matrix with one row per observation. The thresholds are positions on the noise-standardized axis, measured from the mean of the noise distribution (the signal mean sits at d * sqrt((1 + sdratio^2) / 2)), and are not rescaled by sdratio.

metad

Numeric vector. Metacognitive sensitivity (type-2 sensitivity), on the same scale as d (\(d'\), or \(d_a\) when sdratio is not 1), so the M-ratio metad / d is unaffected by sdratio. metad = d corresponds to ideal metacognition (recovers rating SDT).

sdratio

Numeric vector. Ratio of signal to noise standard deviations (default 1, i.e., equal variance). Must be positive. Note that this is the natural scale: the sdratio parameter of sdt_rating() is sampled on the log scale, so it corresponds to log(sdratio) here.

dist

Character. Noise distribution: "normal" (default), "logistic", "gumbel_min", or "gumbel_max".

log

Logical. If TRUE, returns log-density (default FALSE).

n

Integer. Number of observations to generate. n_trials, stimulus, thresholds, and the model parameters are recycled to this length.

n_trials

Integer vector. Number of trials per observation.

Value

dsdt_metad returns the (log-)density (multinomial probability). rsdt_metad returns an integer matrix with one row per observation and one rating-count column per category (r1 ... rK).

Vector arguments

  • r*(n, ...) returns exactly n draws: a vector, or a data frame or matrix with n rows. Every per-observation argument (a parameter, a stimulus, a number of trials) is recycled to length n with rep_len(), as in stats::rnorm(): draw i uses element i, and a matrix is read element by element; only a set of values per draw, such as thresholds, takes row i of a matrix (see below). A shorter vector is repeated, also when n is not a multiple of its length. Until bmm 1.6.0 at the earliest, rddm() with n = 1 and parameter vectors still returns one draw per element, with a deprecation warning.

  • n is a single number of at least 0. A fraction is truncated, as in stats::rnorm(), and n = 0 gives an empty vector, or a matrix or data frame with zero rows and the usual columns. Unlike stats::rnorm(), which takes the length of a vector n, these functions stop on one; rddm() still takes its length, with a deprecation warning.

  • d*(x, ...) returns one value per observation: as many as the longest of x (its rows, when the observations are rows of counts) and the per-observation arguments, the others recycled to that length. Value i is what the call on the i-th elements alone returns. A matrix in an argument that takes one number per observation, such as x or d, holds one observation per element, as in stats::dnorm(). When x or any per-observation argument is empty, the result is empty, as in stats::dnorm(). A NULL argument, such as a misspelt column of a data frame, counts as empty, except where the default is NULL, as for criterion or kcrit: there it means that the argument is not given. Where an observation is a vector of counts (dsdt_rating(), dsdt_dpsdt(), dsdt_metad(), dsdt_ranking() and dsdt_cdp()), or the pair of mean_rt or var_rt values of dezdm(version = "4par"), a vector is always one observation: pass a matrix with zero rows for none, as an empty vector stops. An empty kcrit of dsdt_cdp() and rsdt_cdp() stops as well; kcrit = NULL gives the R/K model. Counts in a data frame, a tibble included, are read as the matrix of its rows, and so are mean_rt and var_rt of dezdm(version = "4par"). dsdm() with a data frame x is the exception: it returns a data frame of the same shape, one density per cell, and cuts longer parameters to the number of cells.

  • A set of values that describes one observation, such as the thresholds of the rating models, is a vector when every observation shares it and a matrix with one row per observation otherwise: row i belongs to observation i, or to draw i.

  • Configuration arguments such as version, dist, log, parametrization and n_new are single values and are never recycled. An argument that a version does not use, such as zr of dezdm(version = "3par"), is ignored.

References

Maniscalco, B., & Lau, H. (2012). A signal detection theoretic approach for estimating metacognitive sensitivity from confidence ratings. Consciousness and Cognition, 21(1), 422–430. doi:10.1016/j.concog.2011.09.021

Examples

# Density for a single observation (K=4) with imperfect metacognition
dsdt_metad(counts = c(5, 15, 25, 55), stimulus = 1,
           d = 1.5, thresholds = c(0.25, 0.75, 1.25), metad = 1.0)
#> [1] 6.662953e-05
# Generate meta-d' rating data (K=4) for 10 subjects and both stimulus types
dat <- expand.grid(id = 1:10, stimulus = c(0L, 1L))
dat <- cbind(dat, rsdt_metad(nrow(dat), 100, dat$stimulus, d = 1.5,
                             thresholds = c(0.25, 0.75, 1.25), metad = 1.0))
head(dat)
#>   id stimulus r1 r2 r3 r4
#> 1  1        0 55 30  8  7
#> 2  2        0 63 13 14 10
#> 3  3        0 60 23  8  9
#> 4  4        0 59 22 12  7
#> 5  5        0 52 21 16 11
#> 6  6        0 66 17  8  9
